prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Two customers are suing Wal-Mart for negligence after being injured in a mad rush for post-Thanksgiving bargains that left one store employee dead, the men's attorney said Tuesday. A temporary worker at this Wal-Mart was crushed to death when shoppers rushed into the store last week. Temporary Wal-Mart worker Jdimytai Damour, 34, was crushed to death as he and other employees attempted to unlock the doors of a store on Long Island at 5 a.m. Friday. Attorney Kenneth Mollins said Fritz Mesadieu and Jonathan Mesadieu were "literally carried from their position outside the store" and are now "suffering from pain in their neck and their back from being caught in that surge of people" that rushed into the Wal-Mart. New York Newsday reported that the Mesadieus are father and son, ages 51 and 19. The lawsuit alleges that the Mesadieus' injuries were a result of "carelessness, recklessness, negligence." In a claim against the Nassau County police department, the men also contend that they "sustained monetary losses as a result of health care and legal expenses ... in the sum of $2 million." "This is a tragic situation that could have and should have been avoided with the exercise of reasonable care. There are very simple measures that could have been put in place to avoid this, such as barriers along the line to spread people out, extra security and a better police presence," Mollins said. He said his clients and others who were at the scene contend that the police "were there ... saw what was happening, and they left." Calls seeking comment from Wal-Mart Stores Inc. were not immediately returned. Lt. Kevin Smith of the Nassau County Police Department said, "it's our policy that we don't comment on open litigations" and would not respond directly to Mollins and his clients' claim that officers left the scene. He said it is "incumbent upon the store to provide security" but noted that there was no security force present when officers responded to an initial phone call after 3 a.m. Friday for an unknown disturbance at the site. Smith said the officers noticed a lack of order with the crowd and began to organize them into a line, remaining on site for about 30 minutes until the crowd had become orderly. Throughout the morning, officers went back to check on the crowd and continued to notice no disturbance, Smith said. He said that there were no additional calls for assistance until about 5 a.m., when people began rushing the doors of the store and trampled Damour. An autopsy showed that Damour died of asphyxiation after being trampled, Nassau County officials have said. Video showed that as many as a dozen people were knocked to the floor in the stampede of people trying to get into the store. The employee was "stepped on by hundreds of people" as other workers attempted to fight their way through the crowd, said Nassau County Police Detective Lt. Michael Fleming. CNN's Kristen Hamill contributed to this report .

NEW YORK (CNN) — An attorney said Tuesday that two Wal-Mart shoppers have filed a negligence lawsuit after they were hurt in a post-Thanksgiving shopping stampede that killed a store employee.

The fatal incident occurred at 5 a.m. Friday at a Long Island Wal-Mart. Jdimytai Damour, a 34-year-old temporary employee, was crushed while he and other workers were trying to open the store’s doors as customers surged inside.

Lawyer Kenneth Mollins said his clients, Fritz Mesadieu and Jonathan Mesadieu, were swept away from where they had been standing outside. He said both men now have neck and back pain after becoming trapped in the wave of shoppers. New York Newsday identified them as a 51-year-old father and his 19-year-old son.

Their lawsuit attributes the injuries to “carelessness, recklessness, negligence.” The Mesadieus also filed a claim against the Nassau County Police Department, alleging that health care and legal costs caused them financial damages totaling $2 million.

Mollins called the event a preventable tragedy, arguing that reasonable precautions—including line barriers to separate the crowd, more security personnel and a stronger police presence—could have stopped it from happening. According to Mollins, his clients and other witnesses maintain that police officers were at the scene, observed the developing situation and then departed.

Wal-Mart Stores Inc. did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Nassau County Police Lt. Kevin Smith declined to address the allegation that officers left, citing the department’s policy against commenting on active litigation. He said stores are responsible for supplying their own security and noted that none was present when police responded to an initial report of an unspecified disturbance shortly after 3 a.m. Friday.

Smith said officers found the crowd disorganized and helped arrange shoppers into a line. They stayed for roughly 30 minutes, leaving after order had been established. Officers returned several times during the morning to monitor the gathering and saw no further problems, he said.

No additional requests for police help came until around 5 a.m., according to Smith. At that point, shoppers charged the entrance and trampled Damour.

Nassau County officials said an autopsy determined that Damour died from asphyxiation caused by the trampling. Video footage showed that up to 12 people were knocked down during the rush to enter the store.

Nassau County Police Detective Lt. Michael Fleming said hundreds of shoppers stepped on Damour while other employees struggled through the crowd in an effort to reach him.

CNN’s Kristen Hamill contributed to the report.

**Two customers sue Wal-Mart over fatal Black Friday stampede**

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** Two customers injured in the Black Friday stampede that killed temporary Wal-Mart worker Jdimytai Damour have filed lawsuits accusing the retailer of failing to provide adequate security and crowd control.

The customers say they were among thousands of shoppers gathered outside a Wal-Mart store in Valley Stream, New York, on November 28, 2008, when the crowd surged through the entrance shortly before the store opened. Their lawsuits seek damages for injuries allegedly suffered in the rush.

Damour, 34, was knocked down and trampled as employees attempted to hold back the crowd. He was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Several other people, including shoppers and store employees, were also injured.

The lawsuits allege Wal-Mart should have anticipated the large turnout and taken additional precautions, such as installing stronger barriers, increasing security and organizing customers into controlled lines.

Wal-Mart has said it was reviewing the claims. Following the incident, the company said it was saddened by Damour’s death and would examine its crowd-management procedures.

The fatal stampede prompted renewed scrutiny of retailers’ Black Friday promotions and the safety measures used to manage large crowds seeking limited-quantity bargains.

### Mesadieu lawsuit over the 2008 Long Island Wal-Mart crowd surge

Fritz Mesadieu and his son, Jonathan Mesadieu, filed a civil lawsuit after being caught in the Black Friday crowd surge at the Wal-Mart in Valley Stream, Long Island, on November 28, 2008. The same surge killed 34-year-old Wal-Mart employee Jdimytai Damour when shoppers broke through the store’s entrance shortly before its 5 a.m. opening.

The Mesadieus alleged that they were knocked down, trampled, and injured as the crowd rushed into the store. Their complaint accused Wal-Mart of negligence for advertising deeply discounted merchandise while failing to provide adequate barriers, trained security personnel, crowd-control procedures, and a safe method for admitting the large crowd.

They also named Nassau County and/or the Nassau County Police Department, alleging that police knew or should have known that the gathering had become dangerous but failed to control or disperse it effectively. As is common in municipal litigation, claims nominally directed at the police department would generally be treated as claims against Nassau County because the department itself may not be a separately suable entity.

The suit sought damages for the Mesadieus’ physical injuries, pain and suffering, and related losses. It was one of several legal actions arising from the incident, including claims by other injured shoppers and Damour’s family.

The broader aftermath included:

- an Occupational Safety and Health Administration citation against Wal-Mart for inadequate crowd management;
- a settlement under which Wal-Mart agreed to improve crowd-control practices and contribute funds to community organizations;
- extensive scrutiny of “doorbuster” promotions and Black Friday safety planning.

The filing itself consisted of allegations, not judicial findings. Public reporting focused mainly on the initiation of the Mesadieus’ claim; a widely reported final verdict specifically resolving their lawsuit does not appear to have followed, suggesting it may have been settled, consolidated, or otherwise disposed of without a prominent published decision.

# Wal-Mart Faces Allegations After Black Friday Crowd Crush Kills Worker

**VALLEY STREAM, N.Y., Nov. 28, 2008** — A temporary Wal-Mart employee was killed and several shoppers were injured early Friday when a crowd waiting for Black Friday bargains surged through the entrance of a Long Island store, knocking workers to the floor and trampling them as the doors opened, authorities said.

The employee, identified as **34-year-old Jdimytai Damour of Queens**, was trying to help control the crowd at the Wal-Mart in the Green Acres shopping complex in Valley Stream shortly before the store’s scheduled 5 a.m. opening. Witnesses said hundreds of customers had gathered outside overnight and pressed against the entrance as opening time approached.

When the doors gave way, shoppers rushed into the building, knocking Damour down. Other employees who tried to reach him were also pushed or knocked over. Damour was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

The Nassau County medical examiner determined that Damour died of **compressional asphyxia**, meaning the pressure of the crowd on his body and chest prevented him from breathing.

Several people injured in the surge later alleged that Wal-Mart had failed to provide adequate security, crowd-control barriers and trained personnel despite promoting heavily discounted merchandise and knowing that a large crowd was likely. The allegations said the retailer’s advertising and sale preparations helped create a foreseeable rush but that the company did not take sufficient steps to organize customers or ensure an orderly entrance.

An attorney representing injured shoppers described the scene as preventable, saying Wal-Mart should have anticipated the danger created by a large, increasingly agitated crowd waiting for limited Black Friday deals. The attorney said the victims would seek to hold the retailer and other responsible parties accountable for inadequate crowd management and security.

Nassau County police treated the store as a crime scene and reviewed surveillance recordings, photographs and witness accounts in an effort to reconstruct the fatal surge. Investigators appealed to shoppers who had witnessed the incident or recorded it to come forward. Police said identifying individuals who may have stepped on Damour would be difficult because of the size and movement of the crowd, but they did not immediately rule out possible criminal charges.

At least four other people, including a pregnant woman, were reported injured. The store was temporarily closed as emergency workers treated the victims and police conducted their investigation.

Wal-Mart said it was saddened by Damour’s death and was cooperating with law enforcement. The company said it had added security personnel and taken crowd-control precautions, but the circumstances surrounding the opening remained under investigation.

The fatality cast a shadow over the unofficial opening of the holiday shopping season and raised urgent questions about retailers’ responsibility to protect employees and customers during heavily promoted, high-volume sales events.

Nassau County police described the scene as “utter chaos,” saying employees trying to hold the doors shut were overwhelmed when the crowd forced its way inside.
